sections.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
sections.body:
The NHS says high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so the only way to find out is to have it measured. Rarely, high blood pressure can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain, the NHS says. NHS inform lists headaches, blurred or double vision, regular nosebleeds and shortness of breath as symptoms of very high blood pressure and says to contact a GP practice if they occur.

For urgent advice, the NHS names NHS 111 for frequent headaches, blurred vision, or chest pain that comes and goes. It says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as this could be a heart attack.

sections.heading: What are the types and causes of high blood pressure?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes primary, or essential, high blood pressure as the most common type, and says it usually develops gradually with age. Secondary high blood pressure is caused by another medical condition or by the use of certain medicines.

MedlinePlus lists chronic kidney disease, disorders of the adrenal gland and pregnancy among the causes of secondary high blood pressure. An NHLBI news item from the US names antidepressants, decongestants, hormonal birth control pills and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen as medicines linked to high blood pressure.

White coat hypertension is the name for readings that run high in the clinic but stay normal outside it. Home or 24-hour monitoring can show whether this is happening.

sections.heading: How is high blood pressure checked and diagnosed?
sections.body:
A blood pressure test usually takes a couple of minutes, according to the NHS. A cuff on the upper arm inflates and then releases. The test may be done a couple of times to make sure the measurement is accurate. The result has two numbers. The top, or systolic, figure is the pressure as the heart pumps. The bottom, or diastolic, figure is the pressure as it rests between beats.

When a clinic reading is high, NICE recommends 24-hour monitoring to confirm the diagnosis, or home monitoring if 24-hour monitoring is declined or not tolerated. The NHS says a doctor or nurse may give a home monitor for use at home.

NICE says investigations for target organ damage should be started while the diagnosis is being confirmed, and that drug treatment may be considered straight away if damage is found.

The NHS says tests are available at pharmacies, GP surgeries and some workplaces.

sections.heading: How is high blood pressure treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says lifestyle changes come first. If those are not enough, or if the risk of other problems is high, medicines are added. Medicine groups named by the NHS and the British Heart Foundation include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics and beta-blockers. The NHS says more than one medicine may be needed to keep blood pressure under control.

Which medicine is offered first depends on age, ethnic background and whether the person has type 2 diabetes. The NHS says beta-blockers are now mainly used when other treatments have not worked.

Blood Pressure UK says dizziness and tiredness are the most commonly reported side effects of blood pressure tablets, and that they often improve or go away as the body adjusts. NHS inform says some people have to take medicine to treat high blood pressure for the rest of their life. The NHS says not to stop taking the medicine if side effects occur, and Blood Pressure UK says that stopping it on its own lets blood pressure go back up.

sections.heading: What can help lower blood pressure day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS describes a healthy, balanced diet, regular activity, weight loss for people who are overweight, cutting back on alcohol and caffeine, and not smoking. Several NHS leaflets say that losing weight helps to lower blood pressure. NHS trust leaflets say that cutting down on salt, ready meals and takeaways helps. One NHS trust leaflet says salt substitutes made from potassium chloride are not suitable for everyone, for example people with kidney problems or heart failure, or those who take certain blood pressure medicines.

The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) advises continuing the treatment plan, having regular follow-up, and learning to monitor blood pressure at home. It adds that the clinician may change or add medicines over time.

sections.heading: What are the complications of high blood pressure?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes high blood pressure as raising the risk of heart disease and stroke. NHS inform names stroke, heart attack, kidney disease and vascular dementia among the problems that untreated high blood pressure can cause. The British Heart Foundation says high blood pressure can lead to complications such as kidney failure, heart failure and vascular dementia.

MedlinePlus says hypertensive heart disease develops because the heart must work harder against the pressure, which over time thickens the heart muscle. A thickened muscle may not get enough oxygen, which can cause chest pain, and without good blood pressure control the heart muscle can weaken and heart failure may develop.

MedlinePlus says the aim of treatment is to lower blood pressure to reduce the risk of related health problems, and that medicines and lifestyle changes can often control it.

faqs.q: Is high blood pressure for life?
faqs.a: NHS inform says some people have to take medicine to treat high blood pressure for the rest of their life. The NHS describes lifestyle changes as the first step, with medicines added if these are not enough or if the risk of other problems is high.

faqs.q: Can blood pressure tablets be stopped if a person feels well?
faqs.a: Blood Pressure UK says that stopping medicine on its own lets blood pressure go back up, and the US CDC says to talk to the health care team or a pharmacist before stopping blood pressure medicine. The NHS says not to stop taking the medicine if side effects occur.

faqs.q: What is white coat hypertension?
faqs.a: White coat hypertension is the name for readings that run high in the clinic but stay normal outside it. Home or 24-hour monitoring can show whether this is happening. An NHS service specification describes 24-hour monitoring as the most accurate method for confirming a diagnosis of high blood pressure, and says it can reduce unnecessary treatment.

faqs.q: Can blood pressure medicines affect pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says some blood pressure medicines may not be suitable in pregnancy, because they can reduce blood flow through the placenta to the baby or affect the baby in other ways. The US NHLBI says women who have high blood pressure during pregnancy are more likely to have high blood pressure later in life.

faqs.q: When does high blood pressure need urgent help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for frequent headaches or blurred vision, or chest pain that comes and goes. It says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness.

keyFacts.value: Usually none, so the NHS says the only way to know is to have it measured.

keyFacts.value: GP surgeries, pharmacies and some workplaces, or with a home monitor that a doctor or nurse may provide.

keyFacts.value: Lifestyle changes, with medicines added if these are not enough.

keyFacts.value: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics and beta-blockers.

keyFacts.value: Call 999 for chest pain that does not go away; NHS 111 for frequent headaches, blurred vision or chest pain that comes and goes.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of type 2 diabetes and how does it develop?
sections.body:
Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms at first, and signs can build slowly over a few years. The NHS lists tiredness, needing to pee more, constant thirst and unintended weight loss as the most common symptoms. Other possible signs are blurred vision, slow-healing cuts, and genital itching or repeated thrush. NHS inform also lists tingling or numbness, which can point to nerve damage.

NHS 111 Wales describes type 2 diabetes as often associated with being overweight or inactive, or with a family history of the condition. The NHS explains that in type 2 diabetes the body either does not make enough insulin or the insulin it makes does not work correctly. NHS 111 Wales advises speaking to a GP about any of these symptoms or about worries over personal risk.

sections.heading: How is type 2 diabetes diagnosed, and what do check-ups involve?
sections.body:
A GP can usually diagnose type 2 diabetes with a blood test and a urine test. NHS Scotland guidance describes HbA1c as the preferred diagnostic test, because it does not require fasting and reflects average blood glucose over the previous few months.

After diagnosis, NICE describes a yearly check-up called the annual review. NICE says it includes checking blood pressure, blood glucose and cardiovascular risk, with regular foot checks, and covers other long-term complications such as kidney and nerve problems. Diabetes UK and NHS material on annual checks also list a urine test for kidney protein and a retinal eye screen. Eye screening is a photograph of the back of the eye, and it is not the same as a routine optician sight test.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for type 2 diabetes?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment usually combines lifestyle changes with medicines. Its treatment page centres on diet, physical activity, weight and smoking, and suggests eating more wholegrains, pulses, fruit and vegetables.

For people without other serious conditions, the NHS describes the usual starting point as metformin together with an SGLT2 inhibitor, which lowers blood sugar by letting extra sugar leave the body in urine. If metformin causes side effects, an SGLT2 inhibitor alone may be recommended. A GLP-1 agonist, given by injection, may be offered to people with a history of heart disease or with obesity when other treatments have not lowered blood sugar enough. Local NHS guidance also describes gliclazide, sitagliptin and pioglitazone as further options.

sections.heading: Can type 2 diabetes go into remission, and when is insulin needed?
sections.body:
Diabetes UK says type 2 diabetes can sometimes go into remission, mainly through weight loss. It avoids the word cure because there is no evidence that remission could remain permanent, and many people who regain weight come out of remission.

The NHS England Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan, using products such as soups and shakes, to eligible people in England who have type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity. NHS England notes that the strict nature of the diet means it is not suitable for everyone. The NHS also advises against very strict low-calorie diets without medical advice, especially for people taking insulin or other diabetes medicines.

The NHS says insulin is prescribed for type 2 diabetes if other diabetes medicines no longer keep blood glucose within a healthy range.

sections.heading: What complications can type 2 diabetes cause, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
Over time, high blood sugar can damage the blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, feet and gums. The NHS lists coronary heart disease and stroke, foot problems where untreated ulcers or infections can lead to amputation, sight problems such as diabetic retinopathy, kidney problems and gum disease. It also says that controlling blood sugar and having regular check-ups is the best way to lower the risk of complications.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and HHS are rare in type 2 diabetes but can be life threatening. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if someone with type 2 diabetes is peeing a lot, feels very thirsty, feels sick, is confused or very sleepy, or is short of breath. NHS inform advises contacting a podiatrist or GP practice urgently for a hot, red, swollen foot or new skin damage, and phoning NHS 111 if the practice is closed.

sections.heading: Living with type 2 diabetes: eating, activity and daily checks
sections.body:
The NHS suggests a healthy diet that includes fruit, vegetables, wholegrain foods such as wholemeal bread and oats, and pulses such as chickpeas and lentils. It also notes that having diabetes increases the harmful effects of smoking.

NICE recommends structured education for adults with type 2 diabetes at the time of diagnosis, with yearly reinforcement and review. Diabetes UK says people should be offered a free diabetes education course. NICE says the care team can point people to support groups, and people can ask for help or advice at any time.

NHS Lanarkshire advises checking the feet every day for cuts, skin breaks or hard skin. NHS 111 Wales says people who take insulin for type 2 diabetes must tell the DVLA, because of the risk of low blood sugar.

faqs.q: Can type 2 diabetes go into remission?
faqs.a: Diabetes UK says type 2 diabetes can sometimes go into remission, mainly through weight loss, though it is not guaranteed to last. The NHS England Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan, using soups and shakes, to eligible people in England with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity.

faqs.q: How is type 2 diabetes different from type 1?
faqs.a: The NHS says that in type 2 diabetes the body either does not make enough insulin or the insulin it makes does not work correctly. MedlinePlus describes type 1 as an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the insulin-producing cells, so little or no insulin is made.

faqs.q: Does everyone with type 2 diabetes need insulin?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment usually combines lifestyle changes with medicines, and that insulin is prescribed if other diabetes medicines no longer keep blood glucose within a healthy range. NHS 111 Wales notes that insulin is not often used in the early years.

faqs.q: Can someone have type 2 diabetes without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says symptoms may come on gradually and not everyone gets them, and NHS inform notes that signs often appear slowly over a few years, so some people do not realise they have it. NHS 111 Wales advises speaking to a GP about any symptoms or worries over risk.

faqs.q: When is type 2 diabetes an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if someone with type 2 diabetes is peeing a lot, feels very thirsty, feels sick, is confused or very sleepy, or is short of breath, as these can signal DKA or HHS. The NHS says both are rare in type 2 diabetes but can be life threatening.

keyFacts.value: The NHS describes metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor as the usual starting point for people without other serious conditions.

keyFacts.value: Tiredness, needing to pee more, constant thirst and unintended weight loss; many people have none at first.

keyFacts.label: How it is found
keyFacts.value: A GP can usually diagnose it with blood and urine tests.

keyFacts.label: Yearly check-up
keyFacts.value: NICE describes an annual review covering blood pressure, blood glucose, cardiovascular risk and foot checks.

keyFacts.label: Long-term risks
keyFacts.value: Damage to blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, feet and gums.

keyFacts.label: Remission
keyFacts.value: Possible for some people; NHS England runs a Path to Remission Programme for eligible people.

keyFacts.label: Emergency route
keyFacts.value: Call 999 or go to A&E if peeing a lot, very thirsty, feeling sick, confused, very sleepy or short of breath.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms and triggers of asthma?
sections.body:
The NHS lists coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness as the main symptoms of asthma. They are often worse at night and early in the morning, or when a trigger is present. Asthma involves swelling, called inflammation, of the breathing tubes that carry air in and out of the lungs.

The NHS says it is not fully understood what causes asthma. Risk factors it lists include a family history of asthma or atopic conditions (conditions linked to allergy), childhood exposure to tobacco smoke, and being born prematurely or at low birth weight.

The NHS lists common triggers such as infections like colds and flu, allergens such as pollen, dust mites and animals, smoke, pollution, weather, mould or damp, and exercise. Some cases are linked to substances in the workplace, which is called occupational asthma.

Asthma + Lung UK says frequent use of a reliever inhaler is a sign that asthma is not well controlled, and advises speaking to a GP, nurse or pharmacist.

sections.heading: How is asthma diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP will typically ask about symptoms and triggers, and may ask about eczema, allergies or a family history of them. There is no single test for asthma. A diagnosis is made from the symptom history and the results of breathing tests.

The NHS lists FeNO, spirometry and peak flow among the main tests. In a FeNO test a person breathes into a machine that measures nitric oxide in the breath, which is a sign of inflammation in the lungs. Spirometry measures airflow and lung volume. Peak flow testing uses a handheld device over a few weeks.

The UK guideline from NICE, BTS and SIGN sets out an order of tests. For children aged 5 to 16 with a history suggestive of asthma, FeNO comes first, followed by spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility. Peak flow measurements over a period of time are used if spirometry is unavailable or delayed.

sections.heading: What are the treatments for asthma?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no cure for asthma, but treatment can help control the symptoms. Inhalers are the main treatment. Reliever inhalers are used when symptoms occur. Preventer inhalers are taken daily to reduce inflammation in the airways.

Asthma + Lung UK explains that a blue reliever inhaler opens the airways but contains no steroid, so it cannot reduce inflammation. The charity says NICE guidelines recommend that no one with asthma should have only a blue reliever inhaler, and that anyone using one also needs a steroid preventer.

Some people use a single combination inhaler called an anti-inflammatory reliever. It contains a steroid and a reliever medicine and is taken only when symptoms appear.

The NHS says tablets may be added if inhalers alone are not controlling symptoms. If asthma is severe and not controlled by inhalers and tablets, injected medicines called biological therapies may be offered. Only an asthma specialist can prescribe them, and they suit only specific types of severe asthma.

sections.heading: Living with asthma: action plans, reviews and outlook
sections.body:
The NHS lists useful steps such as always carrying an inhaler, avoiding known triggers and having vaccinations such as the flu vaccine. A person with asthma will usually have a personal asthma action plan.

Asthma + Lung UK says an action plan helps a person understand their symptoms and what to do if they get worse. It is arranged in traffic-light sections. Green covers everyday care, amber covers worsening symptoms, and red covers the signs of an asthma attack, what to do, when to call 999 and when to contact the GP afterwards.

The NHS says steroid tablets may be used as a short course during an attack, or daily over the long term only in very severe asthma. Long-term or frequent use can cause side effects, including fragile bones (osteoporosis), so people are monitored regularly.

MedlinePlus says there is no cure, but with self-care and medical treatment most people can live normal lives. It adds that symptoms sometimes ease over time, especially in children, and that attacks can be life-threatening and are more common in people with severe asthma.

sections.heading: What happens in an asthma attack, and when should I call 999?
sections.body:
The NHS describes an asthma attack as having severe symptoms and difficulty breathing, which can be life-threatening. NHS 111 Wales lists a reliever inhaler that is not helping, and breathlessness that stops a person speaking, eating or sleeping, as signs of an attack.

NHS 111 Wales advises sitting up, trying to stay calm and taking puffs of the reliever inhaler. It says to call 999 for an ambulance if a person feels worse at any point, or does not feel better after taking the puffs.

NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, such as struggling to speak without pausing, gasping or choking. NHS information also says to contact a GP urgently if a person is more short of breath than usual despite using inhalers as prescribed.

faqs.q: Can asthma be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for asthma, but treatment can help control the symptoms. MedlinePlus says symptoms sometimes ease over time, especially in children, and that with self-care and medical treatment most people can live normal lives. Inhalers are the main treatment.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a reliever and a preventer inhaler?
faqs.a: Reliever inhalers are used when symptoms occur and quickly relax the airways to make breathing easier. Preventer inhalers are taken daily to reduce inflammation in the airways. Asthma + Lung UK says a blue reliever inhaler contains no steroid, so it cannot reduce inflammation, and that anyone using one also needs a steroid preventer.

faqs.q: What tests are used to diagnose asthma?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no single test for asthma. A diagnosis is made from the symptom history and the results of breathing tests. The tests it lists are FeNO, which measures nitric oxide in the breath, spirometry, which measures airflow and lung volume, and peak flow testing with a handheld device over a few weeks.

faqs.q: What is an asthma action plan?
faqs.a: An asthma action plan helps a person understand their symptoms and what to do if they get worse. Asthma + Lung UK describes green sections for everyday care, amber for worsening symptoms and red for an asthma attack. The red section covers the signs of an attack, what to do, when to call 999 and when to contact the GP afterwards.

faqs.q: When does an asthma attack need a 999 call?
faqs.a: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, such as struggling to speak without pausing, gasping or choking. NHS 111 Wales says to call 999 for an ambulance if a person feels worse at any point, or does not feel better after taking puffs of the reliever inhaler.

sections.heading: What does a migraine attack feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS says a migraine attack typically brings a throbbing headache, often on one side of the head, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. The cause is unknown, but a migraine happens when there are changes to nerves and blood vessels in the brain, the NHS says.

An attack can pass through several stages, and not every stage occurs every time. The NHS lists early warning symptoms such as unusual tiredness, yawning, food cravings, mood changes, a stiff neck and needing to pass urine more often. These can start hours, or up to two days, before the headache.

The NHS says about 1 in 3 people with migraine have an aura. It can involve zigzag patterns, flashing lights, pins and needles or difficulty speaking. Aura should not last longer than an hour. The Migraine Trust says recovery after the headache can take hours or days.

sections.heading: What types of migraine are there?
sections.body:
The Migraine Trust says migraine without aura is the most common type. Migraine with aura covers several forms, including brainstem aura, retinal migraine, hemiplegic migraine and silent migraine.

A typical aura involves changes in vision, other sensory symptoms such as tingling, or problems with speaking. NINDS says migraine with brainstem aura needs at least two symptoms during an episode, such as vertigo (a spinning feeling), seeing double, trouble with balance or slurred speech.

The Migraine Trust says some people have aura symptoms but no headache, sometimes called silent migraine. Hemiplegic migraine is a rare, severe type involving temporary weakness or paralysis on one side of the body. In vestibular migraine, vertigo, dizziness or unsteadiness are often the main symptoms. The Trust defines chronic migraine as headache on at least 15 days each month.

sections.heading: How is migraine diagnosed?
sections.body:
NICE says a clinician may ask a person to keep a headache diary to help identify the type of headache. The diary records how often headaches happen, how long and how severe they are, and all medicines taken. NICE advises keeping it for a minimum of eight weeks. For migraine that usually happens around a period, the diary should cover at least the next two periods.

A secondary headache is one where another health problem is behind the headaches. NICE says a person may be referred for tests or to a specialist if this is suspected. NICE lists warning signs such as a head injury in the past three months, headaches that start very suddenly, and speech or balance problems that keep getting worse.

NICE advises against referring people with migraine for brain scans solely for reassurance.

sections.heading: What treatments are there for migraine?
sections.body:
The NHS says migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can help with managing attacks and preventing them. For attacks, the NHS lists painkillers, triptans, gepants and anti-sickness medicine, and advises taking painkillers as soon as the headache starts.

The Migraine Trust says gepants can be an option for people who cannot take triptans or for whom triptans do not work, and that they appear not to cause medication overuse headache. It says gepants, CGRP antibodies and flunarizine are usually prescribed by headache specialists rather than GPs.

For prevention, the NHS lists beta blockers, antidepressants, epilepsy medicines, acupuncture, relaxation techniques, cognitive behavioural therapy and vitamin B2. NHS Scotland guidance also lists candesartan and botulinum toxin for chronic migraine.

The Migraine Trust describes medication overuse headache as a headache caused by taking acute migraine medicines too often. It says over-the-counter painkillers, triptans and opioids can cause it. NICE asks clinicians to be alert to it in people whose headaches developed alongside regular use of pain medicines.

sections.heading: Living with migraine: what helps day to day?
sections.body:
The Migraine Trust says triggers usually combine several factors rather than one cause. It names stress, disrupted sleep and skipped meals among the most common, and says shifts in routine often seem to set off attacks. The NHS names periods, stress, tiredness and certain foods or drinks.

The Trust says too little and too much sleep can each trigger attacks, and that regular bedtimes and wake times may help. Some people have attacks when stress eases, such as at weekends. MedlinePlus, a US health site, says regular sleep, exercise and stress management may help.

Foods such as chocolate and cheese are often blamed, but the Trust says the evidence is thin. MedlinePlus describes a headache diary as a way to find triggers.

sections.heading: When should someone get help for migraine?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for a sudden, extremely painful headache, speech or memory problems, loss of vision or double vision, drowsiness or confusion, a seizure, weakness on one side of the body, or a recent head injury. NHS inform likewise advises calling 999 or going to A&E for one-sided weakness or slurred speech.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if an attack lasts longer than 72 hours, if aura lasts longer than an hour, or if the person is pregnant or has recently given birth.

A non-urgent GP appointment is advised if attacks are severe, getting worse, lasting longer than usual, happening more than once a week, hard to control, or regularly happening around a period.

faqs.q: Can migraine be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can help with managing attacks and preventing them. MedlinePlus likewise says there is no cure, and treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and preventing further attacks. The NHS says the treatments available depend on how severe the migraine is and how often attacks happen.

faqs.q: Is migraine just a bad headache?
faqs.a: The NHS says a migraine attack typically brings a throbbing headache, often on one side of the head, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people also have an aura, such as zigzag patterns, flashing lights or pins and needles. Early symptoms can include tiredness, food cravings and mood changes.

faqs.q: Can someone have an aura without a headache?
faqs.a: Yes. The Migraine Trust says some people have aura symptoms but no headache, which is sometimes called silent migraine or migraine aura without headache, and that it is more common in older people. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if aura lasts longer than an hour.

faqs.q: Is a brain scan needed to diagnose migraine?
faqs.a: NICE advises against referring people diagnosed with migraine for brain scans solely for reassurance. Its quality standard says people with tension-type headache or migraine should not be imaged if they have no signs or symptoms of a secondary headache. A clinician may refer for tests or to a specialist if a secondary cause is suspected.

faqs.q: Can painkillers make headaches worse?
faqs.a: The Migraine Trust describes medication overuse headache as a headache caused by taking acute migraine medicines too often. It says over-the-counter painkillers, triptans and opioids can cause it, while gepants appear not to. The Trust recommends speaking to a GP for anyone taking acute medicines frequently.

keyFacts.value: A throbbing headache, often on one side, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, the NHS says.

keyFacts.value: Migraine without aura, according to the Migraine Trust.

keyFacts.label: Aura
keyFacts.value: About 1 in 3 people with migraine have it, the NHS says, and it should not last longer than an hour.

keyFacts.value: A sudden, extremely painful headache, speech or memory problems, vision loss, confusion, a seizure, weakness on one side or a recent head injury.

sections.heading: What does COPD feel like, and how does it change over time?
sections.body:
The NHS describes COPD as a lung disease that develops slowly, so symptoms are often not noticed early on. The main symptoms are breathlessness during activity, a persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheezing. Phlegm is the thick mucus coughed up from the airways. Several other conditions, such as asthma, heart failure and anaemia, can cause similar symptoms.

The NHS says COPD cannot be cured or reversed. For many people, treatment helps keep it under control so that it does not severely limit daily activities. For some people it keeps getting worse despite treatment and can lead to life-threatening problems. The NHS says that the sooner treatment starts, the less chance there is of severe lung damage.

sections.heading: What are emphysema and chronic bronchitis, and what causes COPD?
sections.body:
COPD is the name for a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties. Emphysema and chronic bronchitis are two of the conditions grouped under it. Chronic bronchitis is inflammation of the airways, which leads to a long-term cough with mucus. Emphysema is damage to the tiny air sacs in the lungs, which reduces the elasticity of the lungs. Many people have features of both.

Smoking is the biggest risk factor. The NHS estimates that it is behind around 9 in 10 cases, and the risk rises with how much and for how long a person smokes. The WHO lists long-term exposure to dust or fumes at work, air pollution, and a rare inherited condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as other factors. In the United States, CDC data show that some adults with COPD have never smoked. The condition usually emerges after the age of 35.

sections.heading: How is COPD diagnosed, and what do the tests show?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP starts by asking about symptoms and about whether the person smokes or used to smoke. The GP examines the chest, listens to the breathing with a stethoscope, may calculate body mass index and asks about any family history of lung problems. The GP may then do, or arrange, a breathing test called spirometry. NICE guidance says COPD is suspected from symptoms and signs, and that spirometry supports the diagnosis.

A chest X-ray can look for other lung problems that cause similar symptoms, such as chest infections and lung cancer, although these do not always show. Blood tests can detect conditions such as anaemia, and sometimes check for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, a rare genetic problem that increases the risk of COPD. A CT scan, which is a detailed scan of the lungs, or a phlegm sample to check for infection is sometimes needed to confirm the diagnosis or judge severity.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for COPD, and what are they for?
sections.body:
The NHS says stopping smoking is the most effective way to prevent COPD getting worse. Damage already done to the lungs and airways cannot be reversed, but giving up smoking can help prevent further damage. Short-acting bronchodilator inhalers, which widen the airways, are usually the first treatment. Long-acting bronchodilator inhalers may be recommended if there are regular symptoms or flare-ups. A GP may add a steroid inhaler if breathlessness or flare-ups continue, and this is normally given in a combination inhaler. NICE favours keeping the number and types of inhalers to a minimum, because that makes it easier to use them correctly. It also says inhalers should only be prescribed after people have been trained to use them.

Pulmonary rehabilitation is a supervised programme of exercise, education and breathing techniques, usually in groups. Oxygen is useful only for people whose blood oxygen is low, and it is not a treatment for breathlessness. Lung volume reduction surgery, which removes badly damaged lung tissue, and lung transplant are options for only a small number of people.

sections.heading: What is a flare-up, and how do people live with COPD?
sections.body:
A flare-up, also called an exacerbation, is a time when symptoms are worse than usual. MedlinePlus describes one as increased symptoms lasting two days or more. Infections are a common cause. Treatment may include quick-relief inhalers, steroids or antibiotics taken by mouth, or oxygen if it is prescribed. Asthma + Lung UK describes an agreed written action plan as central to managing flare-ups. MedlinePlus suggests pursed-lip breathing to save energy, slow the breathing and help a person relax.

Common advice also includes taking medicines as prescribed and avoiding smoke, dust and fumes. The NHS encourages everyone with COPD to have the annual flu jab and the one-off pneumococcal vaccination. NHS Scotland says mental health difficulties are more common in people with COPD than in the general population.

sections.heading: When should someone get medical help with COPD?
sections.body:
The NHS advises contacting a GP about persistent symptoms such as breathlessness, a chesty cough with phlegm or frequent chest infections, especially for someone over 35 who smokes or used to smoke. That is a GP appointment rather than an emergency.

For someone already diagnosed, MedlinePlus lists breathing that is getting harder, faster or shallower, fever, dark mucus, sleepiness, confusion, chest pain or bluish lips or fingertips as reasons to contact a provider. In the UK, urgent but non-emergency advice comes from NHS 111 or the GP the same day. South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust says to call 999 if someone with COPD is very unwell with severe breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood.

faqs.q: Can COPD be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says COPD cannot be cured or reversed, and damage already done to the lungs and airways cannot be undone. For many people, treatment helps keep it under control so that it does not severely limit daily activities. The NHS lists stopping smoking, inhalers and pulmonary rehabilitation among the options.

faqs.q: Is COPD the same as emphysema?
faqs.a: COPD is the name for a group of lung conditions, and emphysema is one of them. Emphysema is damage to the tiny air sacs in the lungs. Chronic bronchitis, which is inflammation of the airways leading to a long-term cough with mucus, is another. Many people have features of both.

faqs.q: Do only smokers get COPD?
faqs.a: No. Smoking is the biggest risk factor, and the NHS estimates it is behind around 9 in 10 cases. Other factors include long-term exposure to dust or fumes at work, air pollution, and a rare inherited condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. CDC data from the United States show that some adults with COPD have never smoked.

faqs.q: What is a COPD flare-up?
faqs.a: A flare-up, or exacerbation, is a time when COPD symptoms are worse than usual. MedlinePlus describes it as increased symptoms lasting two days or more. Infections are a common cause. Asthma + Lung UK describes an agreed written action plan as central to managing flare-ups.

faqs.q: What does pulmonary rehabilitation involve?
faqs.a: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a supervised programme of exercise, education and breathing techniques. It is usually run as group sessions over several weeks, and some people use remote or app-based versions. The NHS lists it among the treatments for COPD, alongside stopping smoking and inhalers.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a stroke?
sections.body:
The NHS uses the FAST test to describe the main signs of a stroke. FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999. The main signs are facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech. Other signs include weakness or numbness down one side of the body, blurred vision, and confusion and memory loss.

The NHS also lists difficulty speaking or finding words, dizziness, a severe headache, and nausea or vomiting among the symptoms. The NHS describes a stroke as a medical emergency and says to call 999 if a stroke is suspected. It says to call 999 even if the symptoms stop, because an assessment in hospital is still needed. A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, causes symptoms like those of a stroke, and the Stroke Association says they usually last from a few minutes to a few hours.

sections.heading: What are the types of stroke?
sections.body:
Ischaemic strokes happen when the blood supply is stopped by a blood clot, and NHS inform says this is the cause in most cases. The NHLBI says the blockage is usually caused by a piece of plaque that builds up in the arteries during some cardiovascular diseases. Haemorrhagic strokes happen when a weakened blood vessel supplying the brain bursts. The NHS says bleeding can occur inside the brain tissue or in the space around it.

A TIA is also called a mini-stroke because the symptoms are temporary. The WHO says a TIA usually lasts only a few minutes and does not cause long-term damage. The Stroke Association describes a TIA as a warning sign, and the CDC calls it a sign of a serious condition that will not go away without medical help. The NHS lists high blood pressure, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and high cholesterol among the risk factors for stroke.

sections.heading: How is a stroke diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says a stroke is diagnosed mainly through blood tests, scans and other checks. It lists CT scans, MRI scans and ultrasound scans to check in and around the brain, and an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the heart. NHS inform says that even when the physical signs of a stroke are obvious, a brain scan is needed.

The scan shows whether a clot or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke, which part of the brain is affected and how severe it is. The Stroke Association says a brain scan should ideally happen soon after arrival at hospital. The CDC says there is no way to know at the start whether symptoms are from a TIA or from a major type of stroke.

sections.heading: How is a stroke treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment depends on the type of stroke. Early treatment may include clot-dissolving medicine, surgery to remove a clot or drain fluid, and a procedure to ease pressure inside the skull. The Stroke Association says thrombolysis uses a clot-busting medicine to break up clots and restore blood flow.

Thrombectomy removes the blood clot to help reduce brain damage by restoring blood flow. NHS inform says it is effective for ischaemic strokes caused by a clot in a large artery in the brain. The NHS says clot-dissolving treatment is most effective when started as soon as possible after the stroke.

The Stroke Association says most people who have an ischaemic stroke are given blood-thinning medication to help prevent clots, and that most will need it for life. NHS inform says a combination of treatments is usually recommended to reduce the risk of another stroke, and long-term prevention can involve anticoagulants or antiplatelets and statins to lower cholesterol.

sections.heading: How long does recovery take, and what does rehabilitation involve?
sections.body:
The NHS says it can take days, weeks, months or years to recover from a stroke. Some people recover within days or weeks, while for others recovery can take months or years and may mean making life changes.

NHS inform describes several kinds of rehabilitation. Physiotherapy often involves exercises to improve muscle strength to overcome walking difficulties. Occupational therapists assess a person’s ability to carry out everyday tasks and can help adapt the home or suggest equipment to make tasks easier. Speech and language therapists help with communication and swallowing problems. NHS inform notes that problems with language can affect speaking, understanding, reading and writing. Rehabilitation usually starts in hospital and can continue at home or in the community.

sections.heading: What problems can follow a stroke, and how do people cope?
sections.body:
The WHO lists trouble swallowing (dysphagia) and aspiration pneumonia, a lung infection, among the complications of stroke. The Stroke Association says being immobile raises the risk of blood clots forming in the leg veins. NHS inform says tiredness can be extreme and can last months or even years, and that bewilderment, anger and frustration are also common.

The Stroke Association says depression is common after a stroke and that at least one third of survivors have some form of it within the first year. NHS inform says medicines and psychological therapies, such as counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), can help some people. The Stroke Association lists its Stroke Helpline as 0303 3033 100.

faqs.q: What does FAST stand for?
faqs.a: FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999, the NHS says. The main signs are facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech. The NHS says to call 999 even if the symptoms stop, because an assessment in hospital is still needed.

faqs.q: Is a TIA the same as a stroke?
faqs.a: A TIA, or mini-stroke, has symptoms like those of a stroke, but the Stroke Association says they usually last from a few minutes to a few hours. The CDC says there is no way to know at the start whether symptoms are from a TIA or a major type of stroke. The Stroke Association describes a TIA as a warning sign.

faqs.q: Which scans are used to diagnose a stroke?
faqs.a: The NHS lists CT scans, MRI scans and ultrasound scans to check in and around the brain, along with blood tests and an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the heart. NHS inform says the scan shows whether a clot or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke, which part of the brain is affected and how severe it is.

faqs.q: How long does it take to recover from a stroke?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can take days, weeks, months or years to recover from a stroke. Some people recover within days or weeks, while for others recovery can take months or years and may mean making life changes. NHS inform describes rehabilitation from physiotherapists, occupational therapists and speech and language therapists.

faqs.q: Can a stroke affect mood?
faqs.a: The Stroke Association says depression is common after a stroke, with at least one third of survivors having some form of it within the first year, and that it can appear at any point or return. NHS inform says anger, frustration and bewilderment are also common, and that medicines and psychological therapies can help some people.

sections.heading: What does heart failure feel like, and how does it progress?
sections.body:
Heart failure means the heart cannot pump blood properly. The NHS says it does not mean the heart has stopped working or is about to stop. Symptoms the NHS lists include breathlessness during everyday activity or when lying down, unusual tiredness, light-headedness, swelling in the feet, ankles, legs or tummy, sudden weight gain and a cough at night. MedlinePlus adds that the pulse may feel fast or irregular.

The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) says symptoms usually get worse as the heart grows weaker. It adds that weight gain, ankle swelling or increasing breathlessness may mean fluid is building up in the body.

NHS 111 Wales describes heart failure as a long-term condition that usually gets slowly worse over time, although it is very difficult to tell how it will progress in any one person.

sections.heading: What are the types of heart failure?
sections.body:
NHLBI says heart failure can develop suddenly, which is called acute, or over time as the heart gets weaker, which is called chronic. It can affect one or both sides of the heart.

NHLBI describes two forms of left-sided heart failure, named after the ejection fraction. This is the percentage of the blood in the left ventricle that is pumped out with each heartbeat. In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, weakened heart muscle is the usual driver. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the ventricle is stiff rather than weak, so it cannot fill with enough blood to pump out to the body.

NHLBI says left-sided heart failure is the main cause of right-sided heart failure, because pressure backs up into the lungs and strains the right side. Other causes of right-sided heart failure include congenital heart defects, abnormal heart valves and lung damage such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

sections.heading: How is heart failure diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP should check the symptoms and offer a blood test to see how well the heart is working. NHS England advises GPs to arrange an NT-proBNP blood test for people with suspected heart failure. NICE says a low result in a person who is not on treatment makes heart failure less likely, while higher results lead to faster referral for specialist assessment and an echocardiogram.

The NHS lists blood tests, an electrocardiogram (ECG), an echocardiogram, breathing tests and a chest X-ray among the tests used. Its main heart failure page also mentions urine tests and MRI scans. An echocardiogram is an ultrasound scan of the heart. NICE says it is used to exclude important valve disease, among other purposes.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for heart failure?
sections.body:
The NHS lists healthy lifestyle changes, medicines, implanted devices and surgery among the treatments for heart failure, and describes medicines as the main one. It says diuretics reduce fluid build-up, ankle swelling and breathlessness, and that beta blockers slow the heart.

Implanted devices can help control or monitor the heart rhythm. They include pacemakers, cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) devices and implantable cardioverter defibrillators. Surgery can repair or replace damaged valves or improve blood flow from blocked arteries. For severe cases, options include a left ventricular assist device and a heart transplant. The NHS says a transplant may be needed when severe heart failure cannot be treated effectively with medicines or other surgery, and that it carries serious risks and is not suitable for everyone.

The NHS says people should be offered an exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme, which often includes education and emotional support.

sections.heading: What is it like living with heart failure?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment will usually need to continue for the rest of life. It describes taking medicines as prescribed, weighing regularly, staying active, eating well and stopping smoking as helpful.

The NHS says people can usually still drink alcohol within the recommended limits, but may be advised to stop completely if their heart failure is directly related to drinking. NHLBI says people may be asked to limit salt and liquids to reduce fluid build-up. The NHS says everyone with heart failure should be offered a flu vaccine every year and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine.

NHLBI says living with heart failure may cause fear, anxiety, depression and stress, and that relaxation techniques, counselling and support groups can help lower stress and anxiety. The NHS says worries can be raised with the GP or care team, and that a heart support group may be useful.

sections.heading: What is the outlook, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
The NHS says that for most people heart failure is a long-term condition that cannot be cured, but treatment can help keep the symptoms under control, possibly for many years. NHLBI says treatment can help many people have a higher quality of life.

The NHS advises booking a GP appointment for symptoms of heart failure. It advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for breathlessness when lying down or during everyday activity, coughing up frothy pink phlegm, or sudden weight gain. The NHS says to call 999 for severe breathlessness, such as gasping, choking or being unable to get words out, for pale, blue or grey lips or skin, or if someone has passed out and is not responding normally. It advises people not to drive themselves to A&E.

faqs.q: Does heart failure mean the heart has stopped?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says heart failure means the heart cannot pump blood properly, but it does not mean the heart has stopped working or is about to stop working. For most people it is a long-term condition, and the NHS says treatment can help keep symptoms under control, possibly for many years.

faqs.q: Can heart failure be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says that for most people heart failure is a long-term condition that cannot be cured. Treatment can help keep symptoms under control, possibly for many years. The NHS says treatment will usually need to continue for the rest of life.

faqs.q: Will treatment be needed for life?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment will usually need to continue for the rest of life. It describes medicines as the main treatment, alongside healthy lifestyle changes. Care teams may suggest daily weighing so that changes in weight are caught quickly, and the NHS lists regular monitoring as part of care.

faqs.q: Who looks after people with heart failure?
faqs.a: A GP usually starts by checking the symptoms and offering a blood test. NICE links a raised NT-proBNP result to referral for specialist assessment and an echocardiogram. The NHS says worries can be raised with the GP or care team, and that a heart support group may be useful. Carers can attend appointments too.

faqs.q: Is exercise part of heart failure care?
faqs.a: The NHS says people with heart failure should be offered an exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme, which often includes education and emotional support. The NHS says everyone with heart failure should be offered a flu vaccine every year and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine.

sections.heading: What does atrial fibrillation feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes atrial fibrillation (AF) as a common heart rhythm problem. It lists palpitations as the most common sign, along with tiredness, breathlessness, dizziness and chest discomfort.

Sometimes there are no symptoms at all. The NHS says the condition may then be found at a routine check-up or when tests are done for something else. NICE guidance advises a manual pulse check to look for an irregular pulse when AF is suspected.

NHS inform describes atrial fibrillation as generally not dangerous in itself, and says many people live normal, healthy lives with it. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) says there is no cure, but people with AF can lead healthy lives.

sections.heading: What are the different types of atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
NHS inform sorts atrial fibrillation into types by how long episodes last. Paroxysmal, or intermittent, AF comes and goes, with episodes lasting from minutes to hours. Persistent AF is when episodes last for more than seven days. Long-term persistent AF is continuous for over a year.

The BHF describes permanent AF as continuous, and says people with it may always have symptoms.

NHS inform adds that some people with atrial fibrillation will still need treatment, or be advised to have it, even though the condition is generally not dangerous in itself.

Some people have episodes that come and go. The NHS says a portable ECG recorder can help diagnose paroxysmal AF, because it can be worn for 24 hours or longer.

sections.heading: How is atrial fibrillation diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if a person thinks they may have symptoms of atrial fibrillation. It also advises contacting the GP if palpitations keep happening or get worse, or if treatment is not controlling the symptoms. A GP may refer a person to a cardiologist, a heart specialist, who checks the heart rate and symptoms.

NICE guidance recommends a manual pulse check to look for an irregular pulse when AF is suspected. It says a 12-lead ECG, a recording of the heart's electrical activity, should be used to confirm the diagnosis. The NHS says an echocardiogram, a chest X-ray or blood tests may also be arranged.

NICE says that when paroxysmal AF is suspected but not found on an ECG, an ambulatory ECG monitor is used, and the choice of monitor depends on how far apart the episodes are.

sections.heading: What treatments are there for atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is currently no cure for atrial fibrillation, but treatment should help manage the symptoms and lower the risk of complications such as blood clots, stroke and heart failure. NHLBI says treatment uses lifestyle changes, medicines and procedures, including surgery, to help prevent blood clots, slow the heartbeat or restore the heart's normal rhythm.

NHS sources list beta blockers and anti-arrhythmic drugs among the medicines for controlling heart rate and rhythm. Anticoagulants are blood-thinning medicines. An NHS trust leaflet says they do not treat the symptoms of AF but do reduce the risk of stroke. Local NHS guidance lists direct-acting oral anticoagulants first, with warfarin for people who cannot take them.

NHS inform lists cardioversion, ablation and a pacemaker among the other treatments. NICE says catheter ablation is usually reserved for people in whom antiarrhythmic drugs have failed. NHLBI describes rhythm control as recommended for people who continue to have symptoms or are not improving on medicines that control heart rate.

sections.heading: How can people live with atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
The BHF says working out what triggers episodes is an important part of self-management. NHS 111 Wales lists caffeine, spicy food, stress, dehydration and lack of sleep as possible triggers.

The BHF says people with permanent AF can generally exercise if they feel well, while people with intermittent AF are advised to exercise only when the heart is in a normal rhythm.

NHLBI says combining weight loss with physical activity and managing other risk factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, alcohol use and smoking, can improve symptoms more than weight loss alone. NHLBI suggests discussing activity levels, weight control and alcohol use with a provider. It also notes that blood thinners carry risks, including the possibility of severe bleeding in the brain.

sections.heading: Is atrial fibrillation serious, and when is it an emergency?
sections.body:
NHLBI says atrial fibrillation that goes undiagnosed or is left untreated can cause serious and even life-threatening complications, including stroke and heart failure. It also lists blood clots, cognitive decline and dementia. The Stroke Association says AF raises the risk of stroke, and that strokes linked to AF tend to cause more brain damage. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says AFib causes about 1 in 7 strokes in the United States.

The NHS says to call 999 for a fast or irregular heartbeat together with chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting or dizziness, or stroke-like signs such as weakness on one side, confusion or difficulty speaking. It advises against driving yourself to A&E. The Stroke Association says to call 999 straight away for any sign of stroke. For symptoms that are not an emergency, the NHS advises seeing a GP.

faqs.q: Can atrial fibrillation be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is currently no cure for atrial fibrillation. Treatment should help manage the symptoms and lower the risk of complications. NHLBI says treatment aims to prevent blood clots, slow the heartbeat or restore the heart's normal rhythm. The options include lifestyle changes, medicines and procedures, such as cardioversion or ablation.

faqs.q: Is atrial fibrillation dangerous?
faqs.a: NHS inform describes atrial fibrillation as generally not dangerous in itself, and says many people live normal, healthy lives with it. However, NHLBI says it can cause serious complications if it is undiagnosed or left untreated. The Stroke Association says it raises the risk of stroke.

faqs.q: Can you have atrial fibrillation without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says sometimes there are no symptoms. The condition may then be found at a routine check-up or when tests are done for something else. NICE guidance advises a manual pulse check to look for an irregular pulse when AF is suspected, and a 12-lead ECG is used to confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: What is the difference between paroxysmal and permanent AF?
faqs.a: NHS inform groups atrial fibrillation by how long episodes last. Paroxysmal AF comes and goes, with episodes lasting from minutes to hours. The BHF describes permanent AF as continuous, with people possibly always having symptoms. Persistent AF lasts for more than seven days, and long-term persistent AF is continuous for over a year.

faqs.q: What can people do to help with atrial fibrillation day to day?
faqs.a: NHLBI says combining weight loss with physical activity and managing risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, alcohol use and smoking can improve symptoms more than weight loss alone. The BHF says working out what triggers episodes is an important part of self-management.

faqs.q: When should someone call 999 about a fast or irregular heartbeat?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for a fast or irregular heartbeat together with chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting or dizziness, or stroke-like signs. It advises against driving yourself to A&E. For palpitations that keep happening or get worse, or if treatment is not controlling symptoms, the NHS advises seeing a GP.
